predecessors.text: Verify that the application enforces access control rules on a trusted service layer, especially if client-side access control is present and could be bypassed.
Verify that trusted enforcement points, such as access control gateways, servers, and serverless functions, enforce access controls. Never enforce access controls on the client.
Verify that the supplied Origin header is not used for authentication or access control decisions, as the Origin header can easily be changed by an attacker.

summaries.body:
The 5.0.0 mapping records V8.3.1 as MODIFIED, moved from 4.0.3 V4.1.1 and covering V1.4.1 and V14.5.2. V4.1.1 required access-control rules to be enforced on a trusted service layer, especially if client-side access control could be bypassed. V1.4.1 required trusted enforcement points (gateways, servers, serverless functions) and said never enforce access controls on the client. V14.5.2 said the Origin header must not be used for authentication or access-control decisions because an attacker can change it. The current clause is that authorization is enforced at a trusted service layer and not via controls an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.

On 15 Feb 2019 elarlang reported that a still-earlier V4.1.1 ("chosen access control solution is flexible enough") duplicated V1.4.2; vanderaj agreed the next day (#442). That is a prior occupant of the V4.1.1 ID, not this trusted-layer clause. Git events on unrelated slots (authentication, V3 session, V11 anti-automation) are noisy; the mapping and predecessor texts are the reliable origin.

On 23 Feb 2019 vanderaj reworded V14.5.2 to resolve #518 (commit b1bf9477). In March 2021 liamsmit made minor wording tweaks to V1.4.1 (commit f9755e50) and jim followed up on the architecture chapter (commit 3b8d3a62). The 5.0 text collapses those three predecessors into one trusted-service-layer rule and names client-side JavaScript as the example of a manipulable control; it does not retain V14.5.2's Origin-header wording.

Issue #436 is about splitting 4.0 V8 logging requirements and does not discuss this authorization clause. Authentication and anti-automation commits on other ID slots do not rewrite it.
